tagline: Castles, engineers, and a reunited nation
overview:
Germany sits at the center of Europe, sharing borders with nine countries, more than any other European nation. It is a little smaller than Montana, reaching from the North Sea and Baltic coasts in the north to the snowy Alps in the south. The capital, Berlin, is a lively city of museums, street art, and history, where a wall once divided East from West. Other great cities include Hamburg, with Europe's third-busiest port, Munich, home of the Oktoberfest, and Frankfurt, a banking hub of skyscrapers.

About 84 million people live in Germany, the most of any country in the European Union, and they speak German. Germany is a federal republic of 16 states with a parliament and a chancellor who runs the government. It has Europe's largest economy, built on engineering: cars, machines, chemicals, and precision instruments carry the label Made in Germany around the world. Germans are known for punctuality, recycling, forests full of hiking trails, hundreds of kinds of bread and sausage, and a history that has shaped the whole modern world.
landAndNature: Northern Germany is flat lowland of heath, lakes, and farmland, with sandy islands and mudflats along the coast where seals rest. The center rises into wooded uplands like the Harz Mountains and the Black Forest, whose dark firs inspired the Grimm brothers' fairy tales. In the far south the Bavarian Alps reach 2,962 meters at the Zugspitze. The Rhine River flows north past castles and vineyards through a gorge dotted with legends, and the Danube begins in the Black Forest on its way to the Black Sea. About a third of Germany is forest. Red deer, wild boar, and foxes are common, wolves have returned to the east, and lynx roam the Bavarian Forest. Lake Constance, shared with Switzerland and Austria, is one of the largest lakes in Central Europe.
peopleAndCulture: Germans bake more than 300 kinds of bread and make some 1,500 kinds of sausage, from Bavarian weisswurst to Berlin's currywurst, eaten with pretzels, sauerkraut, and potato salad. Munich's Oktoberfest is the largest folk festival in the world, and Christmas markets fill town squares with lights, gingerbread, and carved wooden ornaments. Soccer is the national game; Germany has won the men's World Cup four times, and the Bundesliga draws huge crowds. Composers Bach, Beethoven, and Brahms, thinkers like Kant and Einstein, and writers Goethe and the Brothers Grimm were German. Children start school with a giant cone of sweets, the Schultüte. Germans love the outdoors, from hiking to spending Sunday afternoons over coffee and cake.
history: Germanic tribes stopped the Roman legions at the Rhine, and in 800 Charlemagne was crowned emperor of a realm that became the Holy Roman Empire, a patchwork of hundreds of small states. Johannes Gutenberg's printing press around 1450 and Martin Luther's Reformation in 1517 changed the world. Prussia's leader Otto von Bismarck unified Germany in 1871. Defeat in World War I brought hardship, and in 1933 Adolf Hitler and the Nazis seized power, started World War II, and murdered six million Jews and millions of others in the Holocaust. After 1945 Germany was split into democratic West Germany and communist East Germany, divided by the Berlin Wall from 1961. Peaceful protests brought the wall down in 1989, and the two Germanys reunited in 1990. Germany is a leading member of the European Union.
funFacts: Germany has more than 20,000 castles, and Neuschwanstein castle inspired the Sleeping Beauty castle at Disneyland.
The first printed books, automobile, jet engine, and MP3 format were all invented in Germany.
Germany has more than 1,500 kinds of sausage and over 300 kinds of bread, and the bread culture is on UNESCO's heritage list.
There is no general speed limit on many stretches of the German Autobahn highways.
The gummy bear was invented in Bonn in 1922 by Hans Riegel, whose company name came from his initials and his hometown.
